question: Move the AED at P.S. 146 Ann M. Short into a 24/7 outdoor cabinet on the building's street wall.

evidence.text: P.S. 146 Ann M. Short (School, ZIP 10029) has a registered AED at "FRONT ENTRANCE BY SCHOOL SAFETY".
Its hours come from: School building assumed open 7 AM to 6 PM on school days, September to June. Move the school-hours control to test other closing times.
Under that assumption it is reachable 55 of 168 hours in a school-year week, and 0 hours in a summer week if it is a school.
In 2025, an expected 1.18 cardiac-arrest 911 calls a year came from inside its two-minute walking area at hours when every AED in reach was shut (rank 9 of 100 NYC schools).
Within 400 m there are 7 other registered AED locations; 0 of them are open 24/7 by their published hours.
Citywide, a time-blind map puts 4.6% of call-weighted area within a two-minute walk of an AED; at the hour calls actually came in, 1.4% was within reach of one confirmed open.
Published research: a bystander shock with a public AED was associated with survival to discharge of 66.5% versus 43.0% without (Pollack et al., Circulation 2018, observed shockable public arrests).
Overture Maps lists The Mount Sinai Hospital, a hospital normally staffed around the clock, 337 m away: a possible alternative host for a 24/7 AED.
Unknown to this data: cabinet cost, vandalism risk, whether the school already allows after-hours access, and the actual location of each 2025 call inside the ZIP (only ZIP-level data is public).

turns.speaker: advocate
turns.text: Moving this AED to a 24/7 outdoor cabinet addresses a real gap in emergency access. The school currently reaches only 55 of 168 hours weekly during the academic year, and zero hours in summer [E2, E3]. Last year, an expected 1.18 cardiac arrests occurred in the surrounding two-minute walking area during hours when every nearby AED was closed [E4]. Research shows bystander shock with a public AED correlates with 66.5% survival versus 43.0% without one [E7]. The seven other AEDs within 400 meters are all closed after hours [E5], making this location uniquely positioned to serve the community around the clock.

turns.speaker: skeptic
turns.text: The case for moving this AED rests on incomplete data and overlooks a simpler alternative. Yes, the school AED is closed most hours [E2, E3], but we don't know the actual location of last year's 1.18 expected cardiac arrests—only that they fell within the ZIP code [E9]. They may not have been near P.S. 146 at all. Meanwhile, Mount Sinai Hospital sits just 337 meters away and is staffed 24/7 [E8], making it a natural candidate to host a permanent AED instead. Before spending on a street cabinet—whose cost and vandalism risk remain unknown [E9]—the city should verify whether those arrests cluster near this school, confirm Mount Sinai's willingness, and explore whether the school can simply unlock after-hours access. The survival benefit is real [E7], but so is the need to spend wisely on the highest-impact solution.

turns.speaker: advocate
turns.text: The skeptic is right that we lack the precise location of last year's 1.18 arrests within the ZIP code [E9], so we cannot confirm they clustered near P.S. 146 specifically. However, that uncertainty cuts both ways. Mount Sinai's 337-meter distance [E8] may sound close, but it offers no guarantee of faster access than a street-wall cabinet during the critical minutes of cardiac arrest. The skeptic's alternatives—verifying arrest clusters, confirming Mount Sinai's participation, or unlocking school access—all require time and coordination we do not control. A 24/7 cabinet at P.S. 146 removes those dependencies. Given that 1.18 expected arrests occur annually in the surrounding area during hours when every nearby AED is closed [E4], and that bystander shock correlates with 66.5% survival [E7], moving forward with this location addresses the documented gap now rather than waiting for a potentially slower institutional solution.

turns.speaker: skeptic
turns.text: The advocate is right that we shouldn't wait for perfect coordination, but the strongest point cuts the other way: we genuinely don't know whether those 1.18 expected arrests cluster near P.S. 146 or elsewhere in the ZIP [E9]. A street cabinet here could sit unused while the actual need is blocks away. Mount Sinai's 337-meter distance [E8] is not a guess—it's a measurable alternative already staffed 24/7. Before spending on a cabinet whose cost and vandalism risk are unknown [E9], a single call to Mount Sinai takes hours, not months. If they decline, the case for P.S. 146 strengthens. If they accept, we've solved the problem at lower risk. The survival benefit of bystander shock is real [E7], but so is the duty to target it where arrests actually happen.

verdict.summary: Strong evidence supports 24/7 AED access (1.18 annual arrests during closure hours, 66.5% vs 43% survival). However, ZIP-level data prevents confirming whether arrests cluster near P.S. 146 specifically. Mount Sinai alternative at 337m merits rapid exploration before cabinet installation.
verdict.strongestFor: 1.18 expected annual arrests occur when all nearby AEDs closed [E4]; bystander shock yields 66.5% survival vs 43% [E7].
verdict.strongestAgainst: Actual 2025 arrest locations unknown—only ZIP-level data available [E9]; Mount Sinai Hospital 337m away, already 24/7 staffed [E8].
verdict.nextStep: Contact Mount Sinai Hospital within 2 weeks to confirm willingness and feasibility of hosting a 24/7 AED; simultaneously request granular arrest location data.
